content:
According to Mark Gurman's latest Power On newsletter, Apple is reportedly considering several changes to its App Store. The goal? To increase its potential revenue.

Apple's specific plans for App Store changes remain unclear. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports that Apple wants to "find ways to improve profit margins and extract more recurring revenue from the platform," and this effort is being driven primarily by incoming CEO John Ternus and current Services SVP Eddy Cue.

Reportedly, this initiative was also part of the reason veteran Phil Schiller left the company last week. After stepping down as SVP of Marketing in 2020, Schiller took on the Apple Fellow role, with part of his responsibilities including overseeing the App Store. Schiller reportedly had no interest in this idea:

There are many ways Apple could improve App Store margins. For instance, it could eliminate the existing manual app review process—which is costly, though its usefulness may have diminished in the era of agentic coding. However, further automating review work would probably not sit well with users, even though doing so would indeed help reduce costs.

Apple could also raise developer membership fees, which currently stand at US$99 per year. Given that many small developers spend US$200 a month on subscriptions to Codex and Claude to build apps, it's easy to see why Apple would have grounds to hike the price while developers would still happily pay. Apple could also charge large developers subscription fees based on traffic, passing on some of the infrastructure costs.

How everything plays out remains to be seen, but I'm very curious what shape these changes ultimately take.
